view: Asked whether the garden owners were people of Paradise or Hell, Qatada said the question burdened him and gave no answer.

Reports elaborating the garden story say it belonged to a righteous man who left it to his people and town; they variously place it near Sana'a in Yemen, in Abyssinia, or among the People of Scripture.
note: These are reported alternatives, not a single agreed location.

view: Bal shifts from their earlier thought to the more serious fact that, although they meant to deprive the poor of the surplus, they themselves lost all the fruit.
Seeing the ruined garden, they first thought they had lost their way; once they recognized it, they corrected themselves and acknowledged their deprivation.
note: The initial mistake is tied in several notes to the garden's burned, unrecognizable appearance.

view: Their earlier claim of being lost can mean they had gone wrong in planning to harvest while excluding the poor; their correction admits that the expected benefit was lost and their scheme rebounded on them.
note: Razi says they had assumed they could still benefit; Tabatabai describes the error as straying from right conduct. This differs from taking their first claim as a mistaken route.

view: The explicit pronoun is brought forward although the passive construction could leave its subject implicit, restricting true deprivation to them.
Recognizing the garden's landmarks, they admitted deprivation; Muqatil identifies what they saw as punishment, while Ibn Jurayj says they were also afflicted by misfortune.
The declaration recalls 56:67 and extends the lesson to harvests generally: God determines whether crops flourish.
note: The note also mentions 56:63–66 in this connection.

view: The word may also mean that they were rendered destitute.
They were deprived of the garden's fruit, yield, or benefit after its destruction.
note: Ibn Atiyya also names the garden's blessing; Abu Hayyan calls its destroyed produce God's bounty.

view: Their deprivation of the garden was a punishment or consequence of their own wrongdoing.
note: Qatada describes the loss as repayment; Abu Hayyan's report explicitly attributes the destruction to God's punishment.

view: Their attempt or intention to withhold the garden's produce from the poor brought deprivation upon themselves.
note: Some notes describe barring the poor as done; Razi, Biqai, and Ibn Ashur stress the resolve or intention to do so. Abu Hayyan calls its reversal the return of their treachery upon them.

view: Their failure to make an exception contributed to their deprivation of the garden's benefit.
note: Both notes also connect the loss with denying the poor their due.

view: They recognized a punishment and deprivation greater than what they had planned for the poor, and despaired of both their present and future prospects.
A calamity can soften and lead to repentance for a person God intends to guide, while increasing another person's disbelief.
God taking the expected good in response to their changed intention recalls that God does not change a people's condition until they change themselves (13:11).
